doc.title: Roland Hanna interviewed by Monk Rowe, Scottsdale, Arizona, April 15, 2000

chapter: Composing and the Thad Jones band
title: Helping Thad Jones form his band and the stolen tune
summary: Hanna knew Thad from Detroit, gave him the idea for a band in Japan, played the Monday set, and Thad arranged his improvised tune.

story.theme_name: Leading a band: choosing, paying and managing players
story.community_name: Leading a band: running, choosing and keeping players

blocks.x: Thad Jones-Mel Lewis band was a nice career thing for you to do it seems like, and you had some great moments on that record too.

When Thad left the Basie band in 1962 we were neighbors living in the same town. I had known Thad since the 40s from Detroit, Pontiac days you know. Thad lived in Pontiac, I lived in Detroit. And when he left the Basie band he got a gig at Columbia at CBS. His brother Hank was the pianist for Arthur Godfrey and so Hank got Thad a job with the house band there. And it crushed Thad. He had to have a job, but that wasn’t the kind of job — he was hoping it would be something playing jazz. And occasionally Monk would call him, occasionally he’d play with Coleman Hawkins or he’d play with this person around the town, but he wasn’t happy. And so I had a gig at the Five Spot. And I hired Thad. I used to have Coleman come and play with me too. I was friendly with all of them and I would invite them down: Kenny Burrell, anybody. So Thad came and played with me on a regular basis. He came several times. And one night we were playing and some Japanese people came in and they were looking for a group to go to Japan to make a movie. And they came and heard the group and they loved the group and they went around and they heard everybody else and they came back and said look, “We’d like you to come to Japan to make this movie.” So I asked Thad if he would go. And while we were there, now this is in 1963 I think it was, while we were there I talked Thad into getting his own band. And I said look, all you need is a good bass player, good drummer, good piano player. Now I was the leader of that group, but I said I’ll be your piano player if you want to make this band. And I don’t know whether Thad believed me or what. I think he believed me because when he got back he began to write and write more and more. And finally sometime in 1965 he had been working off and on with Mel Lewis and I think the idea that I gave him, he passed it on to Mel Lewis and then they decided to get the band. And I felt kind of left out when he hired Hank, because I had asked him about that first. But it turned out okay, because probably he talked to Hank more than likely, I don’t know for sure. But he probably talked to Hank and said Hank, I hope you can make it but if you can’t man, tell Roland to come on and play. That’s probably why Hank told me to come. So it was a good move. And it was a good move only because Thad wasn’t like Mingus or Sarah or Benny Goodman or anybody else. Thad was open to trying new things. And often times he would let me start out playing, and wouldn’t stop me until half the set was over. So I played the whole set and my chops developed. Richard and Mel behind me, we’d do all kinds of things. Avant garde. In those days they called it avant garde if you’d go out. And we used to go out and come back later. And we did stuff like “Fingers” and “Once Around” and a lot of things that were just really — Every Monday night at the end of the last set, Thad would point to me and say okay you got it. And I would make up, improvise on a tune. Basically it was the same tune for a while, and I’d © Fillius Jazz Archive -15-
just make it up. And then one night Thad came in with an arrangement on this tune. I said, “Thad, isn’t that my tune?” He said no it was mine. He wrote it out.
You should have written it down.
Well see that’s one of those things that there’s no way you can ever re-do that.
Well Ellington did the same thing I hear.
You know he’d hear the guys playing the riffs, and okay.
But I never faulted him for that because he was just doing what band leaders did you know. If you throw an idea out there, he’d take it and write it down.
